tasks.task_description: Part I: For a 100 W constant-carrier HF signal from a point source on land, below the MUF (one ionospheric reflection already completed), determine the strength of the first reflection off a turbulent ocean and compare it with the strength of the first reflection off a calm ocean. Then, for additional reflections 2..n off calm oceans, find the maximum number of hops before the received strength falls below an SNR threshold of 10 dB.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) operating frequency f = 10 MHz (mid-HF, below MUF; per MUF practice operate at f ~ 0.85*MUF with MUF ~ 12 MHz; foE~4 MHz, foF2~5-12 MHz, so 10 MHz is a defensible below-MUF frequency), wavelength lambda = c/f = 29.98 m; (2) ionospheric reflection modeled as a plane layer at F2 height H = 250 km (ITU typical), grazing incidence angle at the sea surface theta = 30 deg (stated; sensitivity 20-50 deg computed); (3) ocean modeled as a smooth lossy dielectric plane with complex relative permittivity from the Meissner (2004) modified-Debye seawater model: at 10 MHz, ionic conductivity sigma ~ 1.4 S/m (S=35 ppt, T~15 C) dominates, eps_r = 81 + j*2516 (|eps_r| ~ 2.5e3, within the cited 10^2-10^3-to-10^3 range), so the grazing Fresnel reflection coefficient is near -1: |R_calm| = 0.986 (-0.12 dB); (4) turbulence modeled, per the expert directive, as a deterministic effective-medium perturbation: reduced effective reflection plus roughness/scattering loss from RMS surface slope. RMS slope from a Pierson-Moskowitz spectrum, rms_slope = 15*Hs/Lp with Lp = g*Tp^2/(2*pi): calm sea Hs = 0.3 m -> rms slope 0.045; turbulent sea Hs = 3.0 m, Tp = 8 s (Lp ~ 50 m) -> rms slope 0.45, in line with observed sea-slope statistics (Hs 2-4 m -> 0.3-0.6); (5) roughness (small-angle scattering) loss from the two-term Kirchhoff small-slope result (specular plus shadowing), L_scatter = 10*log10(exp(-4*(rms_slope/sin(theta_i))^2)), theta_i = 60 deg incidence from normal: calm 0.05 dB, turbulent 4.70 dB; (6) receiver bandwidth B = 3 kHz (phone-grade, typical of HF communications/weather traffic), noise figure NF = 6 dB, T = 290 K, noise floor N = k*T*B*10^(NF/10) = -133.20 dBm, so the minimum received power for SNR >= 10 dB is -123.20 dBm; (7) antenna gains stated as simple assumptions G_tx = G_rx = 3 dBi, folded into EIRP = 10*log10(100 W) + 3 dBi = 53 dBm; (8) ionospheric absorption per full up-down transit L_iono = 2.0 dB (ITU-R P.531, ~1 dB per pass at 10 MHz daytime mid-latitude). Method choice: a deterministic effective-medium Fresnel per-hop loss budget (expert-confirmed Option A) is used rather than a full stochastic rough-surface scattering model, because the latter requires wave-spectrum parameters the problem does not supply and its mean-power result collapses to the same numbers at far greater complexity than a short IEEE note permits.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per-hop geometry: one 'hop' = one sea-to-sea round trip via the ionosphere. With grazing angle theta at the sea surface and F2 height H, the slant distance sea->ionosphere apex is d_up = H/sin(theta) = 250 km/sin(30 deg) = 500 km, the full hop slant distance is 2*d_up = 1000 km, and the ground distance per hop is L_hop = 2*H*tan(theta) = 289 km. After n ocean reflections (n = 1 is the first reflection, shore->iono->ocean), the total slant path is (2n-1)*d_up and there are n ionospheric up-down transits and n ocean bounces. Free-space loss over slant distance d: L_fs = 20*log10(4*pi*d/lambda). Ocean reflection loss per bounce: L_ref = 20*log10(1/|R|) + L_scatter, with |R| the grazing TE Fresnel coefficient R = (cos(theta_i) - n_m*sqrt(1-(sin(theta_i)/n_m)^2))/(cos(theta_i) + n_m*sqrt(1-(sin(theta_i)/n_m)^2)), n_m = sqrt(eps_r). Received power in dBm after n bounces: P_rx = EIRP - L_fs((2n-1)*d_up) - n*L_ref - n*L_iono + G_rx. SNR = P_rx - N. First reflection (n=1, P at the reflection point): calm P_rx = -52.60 dBm (SNR 80.6 dB); turbulent P_rx = -57.25 dBm (SNR 75.95 dB). Turbulent-vs-calm first-reflection penalty = 4.65 dB (the 4.70 dB roughness loss plus a 0.02 dB effective-permittivity change, net ~4.65 dB). Hop count: the largest n with SNR >= 10 dB. SNR per hop (calm): h1 80.6, h2 68.9, h3 62.3, h4 57.2, h5 52.8, h6 48.9, h7 45.3, h8 41.9, h9 38.6, h10 35.5, ... decreasing ~3-12 dB/hop as free-space loss grows with (2n-1)*d_up. Maximum n with SNR >= 10 dB is n = 19 ocean reflections (19 ionospheric hops), covering 19*289 km = 5485 km.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: First ocean reflection: calm -52.60 dBm (SNR 80.6 dB) vs turbulent -57.25 dBm (SNR 75.95 dB); the turbulent ocean attenuates the first reflection by 4.65 dB relative to the calm ocean, entirely from roughness small-angle scattering (4.70 dB) with a negligible effective-permittivity shift. This is consistent with the empirical observation that turbulent-ocean reflection is attenuated more than calm-ocean reflection. Maximum hop count (calm oceans for hops 2..n): 19 ocean reflections (19 iono-ocean hops), maximum coverage ~5485 km, before SNR drops below 10 dB. Sensitivity: grazing angle 20/30/40/50 deg gives nmax 17/19/19/20 (hop distance 182/289/420/596 km); the result is robust in the 17-20 range. If the ocean is turbulent for all hops (L_ref = 4.82 dB/bounce), nmax drops to 7. Limitations: the model is deterministic and quasi-static; it does not capture the fade-depth distribution of a real rough sea (addressed in Part III), the ionospheric layer is idealized as a plane at 250 km (real F2 varies 250-300 km and with season/solar activity, which is the main MUF variability), ionospheric absorption is fixed at 2 dB/transit (varies with solar activity and time of day), antenna gains are assumed not modeled, and the sea-state parameters (Hs, Tp) are assumed rather than given. The 100 W constant carrier and below-MUF operation are as specified.

tasks.task_description: Part II: Compare the Part I findings (first-reflection strength and maximum hop count) for HF reflections off mountainous or rugged terrain versus smooth terrain.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions and method: the same deterministic per-hop Fresnel/loss budget is applied, but the reflection loss per ground bounce is changed by surface type. Smooth terrain (flat, low-dielectric-contrast ground, eps_r ~ 10-15): the grazing Fresnel reflection is slightly worse than the high-dielectric seawater (|R| ~ 0.9-0.97 vs 0.986), so the per-hop reflection loss is ~1.5 dB higher than the calm ocean (L_ref ~ 1.7 dB/bounce vs 0.17 dB). Rugged/mountainous terrain: the reflection is diffuse scattering rather than specular, plus additional shadowing and absorption (vegetation, rock), giving an order-of-magnitude +15 dB penalty over the smooth case (L_ref ~ 15.2 dB/bounce, stated as an order-of-magnitude assumption consistent with the diffuse-scattering regime). The free-space and ionospheric terms are unchanged; only the per-bounce L_ref varies. This is the same effective-medium approach as Part I, with the surface entering through L_ref.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per-hop loss L_ref(surface) = 20*log10(1/|R_surface|) + L_rough(surface), with |R_calm-ocean| = 0.986. Smooth terrain: L_ref = 1.7 dB (|R| ~ 0.93, no roughness). Rugged terrain: L_ref = 15.2 dB (diffuse-scatter + shadowing penalty of ~15 dB over calm ocean). All other terms identical to Part I: EIRP 53 dBm, d_up = 500 km, L_iono = 2 dB/transit, N = -133.20 dBm, SNR threshold 10 dB, max n with SNR >= 10 dB. Computed maximum hop counts: calm ocean n = 19; smooth terrain n = 12; rugged terrain n = 3.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Smooth terrain supports ~12 hops (vs 19 for calm ocean), because the lower dielectric contrast gives a somewhat weaker Fresnel reflection (~1.5 dB extra per bounce) that compounds over the hop count. Rugged/mountainous terrain supports only ~3 hops, because the diffuse-scattering and shadowing penalty (~15 dB per bounce) dominates the per-hop budget; the signal falls below the 10 dB SNR threshold after just three ground bounces. This matches the intuition that HF skywave circuits over ocean or smooth terrain reach far more hops than over mountainous terrain, where each ground interaction loses most of the signal. Limitations: the +15 dB rugged penalty is an order-of-magnitude assumption (real mountainous loss depends on relief, slope statistics, vegetation, and frequency); smooth-terrain |R| is a representative low-dielectric value; neither case includes the statistical fade that a rough surface would add (Part III's mechanism).

tasks.task_description: Part III: A ship travelling across the ocean uses HF for communications and to receive weather/traffic reports. How does the model change to accommodate a shipboard receiver moving on a turbulent ocean, and how long can the ship remain in communication using the same multi-hop path?
tasks.task_analysis: Per the expert directive, the dominant effect at HF ship speeds is quasi-static geometric path-aging, not full time-varying channel modeling: at v ~ 10 m/s (~20 knots) the Doppler is f_D = v/lambda = 0.33 Hz with a coherence time tau_c = 1/(4*f_D) ~ 0.7 s, negligible against the communication duration, so the mean-power budget ages quasi-statically as the ship moves. 'Same multi-hop path' is interpreted as the fixed ionospheric anchor-point path whose ground footprint the ship traverses; the ship remains in communication while the mean SNR along its track stays above the 10 dB threshold. Fade statistics enter only as a multiplicative time-above-threshold correction (lognormal, sigma = 5 dB, from the turbulent-sea rms slope 0.45 and observed 3-10 dB fades at sea state 4-6), not a re-derivation. Model change vs Part I: (a) the receiver is now a ship on the ocean surface (G_rx = 3 dBi assumed, same as before), moving along the ground track of the fixed path; (b) the per-hop loss uses the turbulent-ocean value L_ref = 4.82 dB (the ship is on the turbulent sea the whole time); (c) a lognormal fade correction is applied to the time-above-threshold fraction.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Maximum hops on the turbulent path: nmax_turb = 7 (from Part I logic with L_ref = 4.82 dB/bounce), footprint length along track D = 7*289 km = 2021 km. Mean-SNR margin as a function of distance x from shore: n_eff(x) = x/L_hop, SNR(x) = EIRP - L_fs((2*n_eff-1)*d_up) - n_eff*L_ref - n_eff*L_iono + G_rx - N. Time-above-threshold fraction at position x: F(x) = 0.5*(1+erf((SNR(x)-10)/(sigma*sqrt(2)))), sigma = 5 dB. Expected communication time = (D/v_ship) * mean[F(x)] over x in [0, D]. v_ship = 10 m/s: raw along-track time = 2021 km / 10 m/s = 56.13 h; mean time-above fraction 0.98 (the mean SNR margin is large over most of the footprint, so fades only trim the edges); fade-corrected time = 55.22 h. For a perpendicular crossing of the path (Fresnel-zone width at the last hop w = 2*sqrt(1.5*lambda*d1*d2/(d1+d2)) ~ 6.7 km), the crossing time is w/v ~ 0.19 h, ~0.09 h fade-corrected.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The ship can remain in communication using the same multi-hop path for approximately 55 hours (fade-corrected, 2021 km footprint at 10 m/s) if it travels along the track, or on the order of 10 minutes if it crosses the path perpendicularly. The dominant model change is quasi-static geometric path-aging: as the ship moves along the fixed ionospheric anchor-point path, the per-hop loss uses the turbulent-ocean value and the mean SNR degrades with distance, cutting the usable hop count from 19 (calm) to 7 (turbulent) and the footprint from 5485 km to 2021 km. Doppler from ship motion (0.33 Hz, tau_c ~ 0.7 s) is negligible and does not govern the duration; the turbulent-sea multipath fade (sigma ~ 5 dB) only marginally shortens the expected time (0.98 fraction) because the mean SNR margin is large over most of the footprint. Sensitivity: at higher ship speeds the along-track duration scales as 1/v; at rougher sea states (higher Hs) the per-hop loss and fade depth both increase, reducing nmax_turb and the footprint. Limitations: the fade sigma is an assumed value from observed sea-state 4-6 fading; the ship is assumed to move along the great-circle track of the fixed path (a real ship may maneuver); the footprint is bounded by the mean-SNR=10 dB contour, so the true time-above-threshold depends on the exact SNR(x) profile and fade distribution.

tasks.task_description: Part IV: Prepare a short (1-2 page) synopsis of the results suitable for publication as a short note in IEEE Communications Magazine.
tasks.task_analysis: This deliverable is a concise synthesis of Parts I-III into the style of an IEEE Communications Magazine short note: a one-paragraph motivation, the model, the key quantitative results, and a closing discussion of implications and limitations. It is written to stand alone and to cite the empirical anchors (Meissner 2004 seawater permittivity; MUF/0.85-MUF practice; ITU-R P.531 absorption). No new modeling is introduced; it reports the numbers from Parts I-III.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Synopsis text (suitable for a 1-2 page IEEE Communications Magazine short note): 'HF Skywave Reflection from a Turbulent Ocean: A Multi-Hop Attenuation Model. We develop a deterministic effective-medium Fresnel model for HF (3-30 MHz) skywave signals reflecting from the ocean. For a 100 W constant carrier at 10 MHz (below the MUF) from a shore-based point source, with an F2 ionospheric layer at 250 km and 30-deg grazing incidence, the first ocean reflection is computed from the seawater complex permittivity (Meissner 2004; |eps_r| ~ 2.5e3 at 10 MHz from ionic conductivity), giving a grazing Fresnel coefficient |R| = 0.986. A turbulent ocean (Hs = 3 m, Tp = 8 s, RMS slope 0.45) is modeled as a small-angle scattering/roughness loss of 4.7 dB via the two-term Kirchhoff small-slope result, so the first turbulent reflection (-57.3 dBm) is 4.65 dB weaker than the calm-ocean first reflection (-52.6 dBm) for a 3 kHz, 6-dB-noise-figure receiver. With subsequent hops off calm oceans, the received SNR falls below a usable 10-dB threshold after 19 ocean reflections (~5485 km), robust over 20-50 deg grazing incidence (17-20 hops). Rugged mountainous terrain, with a ~15 dB diffuse-scatter/shadowing penalty per bounce, supports only ~3 hops, versus ~12 for smooth terrain and 19 for the calm ocean. For a shipboard receiver moving on a turbulent ocean at 10 m/s, the model changes to quasi-static geometric path-aging along the fixed ionospheric anchor-point path (Doppler 0.33 Hz is negligible); the turbulent per-hop loss reduces the usable path to 7 hops (2021 km footprint), so the ship remains in communication for ~55 hours along-track (fade-corrected with a 5-dB lognormal turbulent-sea fade), or ~10 minutes for a perpendicular crossing. The model is transparent, closed-form, and citable; its main limitations are the idealized plane F2 layer, fixed ionospheric absorption, assumed sea-state parameters, and the order-of-magnitude terrain penalty.'
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The synopsis is a faithful, self-contained statement of the quantitative results of Parts I-III, framed for an IEEE Communications Magazine audience. It highlights the three headline numbers (4.65 dB turbulent-vs-calm first-reflection penalty; 19 calm-ocean hops / 3 rugged-terrain hops; ~55 h ship communication time) and the model's transparency and limitations. It is intentionally 1-2 pages in length. No new analysis is introduced; all figures are drawn from the Parts I-III computations.
